paragraphs: This was the third time Ivan had gone to see Smerdyakov since coming back from Moscow. He had seen and talked to him the first time on the very day he arrived, and then he had visited him once more, two weeks later. After that second visit he stopped going, so it was now over a month since he had last seen him. And he had hardly heard anything about him.

Ivan had only returned five days after his father’s death, so he had missed the funeral, which took place the day before he got back. The delay came about because Alyosha did not know his Moscow address. He had to ask Katerina Ivanovna to telegraph him, and she did not know the address either. So she telegraphed her sister and aunt, counting on Ivan to visit them as soon as he reached Moscow. But he did not go to them until four days after he arrived. When he got the telegram, he naturally set off for our town at once. Alyosha was the first to meet him. Ivan was greatly surprised to find that Alyosha, against the opinion of the whole town, refused to suspect Mitya and spoke openly of Smerdyakov as the murderer. Later he saw the police captain and the prosecutor and heard the details of the charge and the arrest, and then he was more surprised at Alyosha still. He put Alyosha’s opinion down to nothing but exaggerated brotherly feeling and sympathy for Mitya, of whom Alyosha, as Ivan knew, was very fond.

By the way, let me say a word or two about Ivan’s feeling for his brother Dmitri. He simply disliked him. At most he felt a certain pity for him at times, and even that was mixed with great contempt, almost revulsion. Everything about Mitya, even his appearance, was extremely unattractive to him. Ivan looked with indignation on Katerina Ivanovna’s love for his brother. Yet he went to see Mitya on the very day he arrived, and that meeting, far from shaking Ivan’s belief in his guilt, only strengthened it. He found his brother agitated and nervously excited. Mitya had been talkative, but very absent-minded and incoherent. He used violent language, accused Smerdyakov, and was dreadfully muddled. He talked mostly about the three thousand roubles, which he said his father had “stolen” from him.
“The money was mine, it was my money,” Mitya kept repeating. “Even if I had stolen it, I’d have had the right.”

He hardly disputed the evidence against him, and when he tried to turn some fact to his advantage, he did it in an absurd and incoherent way. He hardly seemed to want to defend himself, whether to Ivan or to anyone else. Quite the contrary: he was angry and proudly scornful of the charges, and kept flaring up and abusing everyone. He only laughed contemptuously at Grigory’s testimony about the open door and declared that “the devil opened it.” But he could offer no coherent explanation of the fact. He even managed to insult Ivan during that first meeting, telling him sharply that people who declared that “everything was lawful” had no business suspecting and questioning him. All in all, he was anything but friendly to Ivan on that occasion. Right after that visit to Mitya, Ivan went for the first time to see Smerdyakov.

On the train from Moscow he had kept thinking about Smerdyakov and about his last conversation with him, on the evening before he went away. Many things in it seemed to him puzzling and suspicious. But when he gave his testimony to the investigating lawyer, Ivan said nothing about that conversation for the time being. He put it off until he had seen Smerdyakov, who was then in the hospital.

Doctor Herzenstube and Varvinsky, the doctor he met at the hospital, answered Ivan’s persistent questions by insisting that Smerdyakov’s epileptic attack was unmistakably genuine. They were even surprised that Ivan asked whether he might have been shamming on the day of the catastrophe. They made it clear that the attack had been an exceptional one. The fits had kept coming back several times, so that the patient’s life was really in danger, and only now, after treatment, could they say with confidence that he would survive. “Though it may well be,” added Doctor Herzenstube, “that his mind will be impaired for a considerable time, if not permanently.” Ivan asked impatiently whether that meant he was mad now. They told him that this was not yet so, in the full sense of the word, but that certain abnormalities could be noticed. Ivan decided to find out for himself what those abnormalities were.

At the hospital he was allowed to see the patient at once. Smerdyakov was lying on a low narrow bed in a separate ward. There was only one other bed in the room. In it lay a tradesman of the town, swollen with dropsy and obviously almost dying, so he could be no hindrance to their conversation. Smerdyakov grinned uncertainly when he saw Ivan, and for the first instant seemed nervous. So at least Ivan thought. But that lasted only a moment. For the rest of the time Ivan was struck, on the contrary, by Smerdyakov’s composure. From the first glance he had no doubt that the man was very ill. He was very weak. He spoke slowly, as if moving his tongue with difficulty. He was much thinner and sallower. Throughout the interview, which lasted twenty minutes, he kept complaining of a headache and of pain in all his limbs. His thin, unmanly face seemed to have shrunk to something tiny. His hair was ruffled, and the crest of curls at the front stood up in a thin tuft. But the left eye, screwed up and seeming to insinuate something, showed Smerdyakov unchanged. “It’s always worth while speaking to a clever man.” Ivan was reminded of that at once. He sat down on the stool at the foot of the bed. Smerdyakov, with painful effort, shifted his position, but he did not speak first. He stayed silent and did not even look very interested.
“Can you talk to me?” asked Ivan. “I won’t tire you much.”
“Certainly I can,” mumbled Smerdyakov in a faint voice. “Have you been back long, your honor?” he added in a patronizing way, as though encouraging a nervous visitor.
“I only arrived today.... To see the mess you’re in.”
Smerdyakov sighed.
“Why do you sigh? You knew about it all along,” Ivan blurted out.
Smerdyakov stayed stolidly silent for a while.
“How could I help knowing? It was clear beforehand. But how could I tell it would turn out like that?”
“What would turn out? Don’t evade the question! You predicted you’d have a fit, on the way down to the cellar, remember. You named the very spot.”
“Have you said so at the examination yet?” Smerdyakov asked calmly.
Ivan suddenly felt angry.
“No, I haven’t yet, but I certainly will. You have a great deal to explain to me, my man, and let me tell you, I won’t let you play games with me!”
“Why would I play games with you, when I trust you completely, as I would God Almighty?” said Smerdyakov, just as calmly, closing his eyes for a moment only.

“In the first place,” began Ivan, “I know that epileptic fits can’t be predicted. I’ve asked. Don’t try to fool me. You can’t foretell the day and the hour. So how did you tell me the day and the hour beforehand, and the cellar too? How could you know you’d fall down the cellar stairs in a fit, unless you faked the fit on purpose?”

“I had to go down to the cellar anyway, several times a day in fact,” Smerdyakov drawled deliberately. “I fell from the garret in just the same way a year ago. It’s quite true you can’t tell the day and hour of a fit beforehand, but you can always have a presentiment of it.”
“But you did foretell the day and the hour!”
“About my epilepsy, sir, you’d do much better to ask the doctors here. You can ask them whether it was a real fit or a sham. There’s no use my saying any more about it.”
“And the cellar? How could you know about the cellar beforehand?”

“You can’t seem to get over that cellar! As I was going down to it, I was in terrible dread and doubt. What frightened me most was losing you and being left without defense in all the world. So I went down into the cellar thinking, ‘Here, it’ll come on any moment, it’ll strike me down any moment, shall I fall?’ And it was through this fear that I suddenly felt the spasm that always comes ... and so I went flying. All that, and all my earlier conversation with you at the gate the evening before, when I told you how frightened I was and spoke of the cellar, I told to Doctor Herzenstube and to Nikolay Parfenovitch, the investigating lawyer, and it’s all been written down in the official record. And the doctor here, Mr. Varvinsky, maintained to all of them that it was just the thought of it that brought it on, the apprehension that I might fall. It was just then that the fit seized me. And so they’ve written it down that this is how it must have happened, simply from my fear.”
When he finished, Smerdyakov drew a deep breath, as if worn out.

“Then you’ve said all that in your testimony?” said Ivan, somewhat taken aback. He had meant to frighten him with a threat to repeat their conversation, and it turned out that Smerdyakov had already reported it all himself.
“What have I got to be afraid of? Let them write down the whole truth,” Smerdyakov declared firmly.
“And have you told them every word of our conversation at the gate?”
“No, not every single word.”
“And did you tell them that you can sham fits, as you boasted then?”
“No, I didn’t tell them that either.”
“Tell me now, why did you send me to Tchermashnya then?”
“I was afraid you’d go away to Moscow. Tchermashnya is nearer, anyway.”
“You’re lying. You suggested my going away yourself. You told me to get out of the way of trouble.”

“That was simply out of affection and my sincere devotion to you, because I foresaw trouble in the house and wanted to spare you. Only I wanted to spare myself even more. That’s why I told you to get out of harm’s way, so that you’d understand there would be trouble in the house and would stay at home to protect your father.”
“You could have said it more plainly, you blockhead!” Ivan suddenly flared up.

“How could I have said it more plainly then? It was simply my fear that made me speak, and you might have been angry, too. I might well have been apprehensive that Dmitri Fyodorovitch would make a scene and carry off that money, for he considered it as good as his own. But who could have known it would end in a murder like this? I thought he would only carry off the three thousand that lay under the master’s mattress in the envelope, and you see, he’s murdered him. How could you have guessed it either, sir?”
“But if you say yourself that it couldn’t be guessed, how could I have guessed and stayed at home? You contradict yourself!” said Ivan, thinking it over.
“You might have guessed from my sending you to Tchermashnya and not to Moscow.”
“How could I guess it from that?”
Smerdyakov seemed very tired, and he was silent again for a minute.

“You might have guessed from my asking you to go not to Moscow but to Tchermashnya that I wanted to have you nearer, for Moscow is a long way off, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch, knowing you were not far away, would not be so bold. And if anything had happened, you might have come to protect me, too, for I warned you about Grigory Vassilyevitch’s illness, and that I was afraid of having a fit. And when I explained those knocks to you, by which one could get in to the deceased, and that Dmitri Fyodorovitch knew them all through me, I thought you would guess for yourself that he would be sure to do something. So you would not go even to Tchermashnya, but would stay.”
